events.detail: Rides with West from Oyster Bay to Smithtown
Afternoon ride on to Lake Ronkonkoma for supper
Returns to Smithtown for the night

tr_quotes.text: In all about 35 miles and the horse as fresh as when he started.

headline: Back from Smithtown in the heat
summary: Roosevelt rides home from Smithtown to Oyster Bay in two and a half hours on a very hot day.

events.detail: Rides from Smithtown back to Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: Very hot.

uncertain: The diary says 'we' but does not name his companion; presumably West.

headline: Twenty-five miles by oar to Rye
summary: Leaving at 5:15 a.m., Roosevelt rows across to Rye Beach by way of Rocky Point and Oak Bluff, then rows home that evening, a round trip of more than 25 miles in calm, heavy heat. He spots a stormy petrel.

events.detail: Rows from Oyster Bay to Rye Beach and back, over 25 miles
Sees a stormy petrel

tr_quotes.text: In all I rowed rather over 25 miles.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: A one-line Sunday prayer
summary: Roosevelt's diary for this Sunday holds a single line of scripture, a plea from the Gospel of Mark.

events.detail: Records a Biblical prayer in his diary

tr_quotes.text: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief!

headline: Woodcock in the woods
summary: Roosevelt hikes far through woods and fields with his shotgun and brings back four woodcock and two doves.

events.detail: Long hunting walk, bagging four woodcock and two doves

uncertain: Bag tally OCR'd as '41 woodcock'; read as 4.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Visiting the sick, then the Dickeys
summary: In New York City Roosevelt calls on his ailing friend Cassin, then spends the evening with the Dickey family, whose warmth he loves. Young Charles Dickey will enter Harvard next year, and Roosevelt promises himself to help him.

events.detail: Goes into New York City
Visits Cassin, who is ill
Evening with the Dickey family

tr_quotes.text: I like them ever so much, they are so sweet and homelike.

uncertain: Location of the Dickeys' home is not stated beyond 'out here'.

headline: Home again to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt heads back out to Oyster Bay from his stay near the city.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: Returned to Oyster Bay.

headline: Rigging a sail on his skiff
summary: Roosevelt fits his small outrigger skiff with a leg-of-mutton sail on a seven-foot mast and takes her out. She points poorly into the wind but holds steady and moves briskly downwind.

events.detail: Rigs a sail on his lapstreak skiff and takes her out

tr_quotes.text: She beats very badly, but is stiff and sails pretty fast off the wind.

uncertain: Header OCR'd 'QYSTER BAY'; 'rail' in source is presumably 'sail'.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Marsh shooting on Alice Lee's birthday
summary: On the day Alice Lee, his future wife, turns 17, Roosevelt rows to Lloyd Neck and paddles the winding marsh channels at high tide, taking shots at herons and snipe. A southerly breeze lets him sail several miles out into the Sound. Elliott leaves on a three-week holiday.

events.detail: Rows to Lloyd Neck and shoots through the marsh, getting three sand snipe
Sails three or four miles into Long Island Sound
Elliott departs for a three-week holiday
Alice Lee turns 17

tr_quotes.text: At high tide it is good fun to paddle through the lagoons and among the winding channels, with an occasional shot at a heron or snipe.

uncertain: 'Chuf fF [Ellie]' read as Elliott.

headline: Rainy woods, then a fine ride
summary: Despite rain, Roosevelt roams the woods with his gun in the morning, bagging a dove and a wild pigeon, and enjoys a splendid ride in the afternoon.

events.detail: Morning walk with his gun; one dove and one wild pigeon
Afternoon horseback ride

headline: Quick row around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt borrows Alfred's boat and circles Centre Island in an hour and 24 minutes.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island in 1 hour 24 minutes

tr_quotes.text: Rowed round Centre Island in Alfred's boat in 1h 24m.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Timed circuit of Lloyd Neck
summary: Starting at ten, Roosevelt rows around Lloyd Neck past the Huntington Harbor lighthouse and is home by 1:45. A dead-high tide trims the portage to four minutes.

events.detail: Rows around Lloyd Neck, passing Huntington Harbor lighthouse

tr_quotes.text: Portage took but four minutes, tide being dead high.

headline: Aiming for Greenwich, landing in Darien
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen sail across the Sound meaning to reach Greenwich but misjudge which side of Shippan Point to pass and end up at Darien. Roosevelt notes he has ridden his horse every day he has been home this season.

events.detail: Sails across the Sound with Emlen, missing Greenwich and fetching Darien
Has ridden his horse daily all summer

tr_quotes.text: My horse has done wonderfully this season; I have not missed riding him a single day when at home

headline: Doers of the word
summary: Roosevelt admires the scripture carved over his church door and writes that he puts no stock in faith without deeds. He has been reading the published memorial to his father and resolves to live as his father would have hoped.

events.detail: Reflects on the church motto about acting on faith
Reads the memorial volume to his late father

tr_quotes.text: I am no believer in faith without works.
With Gods help I shall try to lead such a life as Father would have wished me to.

headline: Woodcock in thick cover
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock over some 25 miles of rough country, where the birds now hide in dense brush. He misses more than half his shots and comes home with seven, he and the dog both worn out by the heat.

events.detail: Tramps about 25 miles after woodcock, killing seven

tr_quotes.text: I shot wretchedly; missing over half my birds.

headline: A birthday gift for Edith Carow
summary: For Edith Carow's 17th birthday, Roosevelt sends her a bonbonniere. His sister Corinne also writes Edith an affectionate letter about her future.

events.detail: Sends Edith Carow a bonbonniere for her birthday
Corinne writes warmly to Edith

tr_quotes.text: It being Edith C's 17th birthday, I sent her a bonbonierre

uncertain: Corinne's letter is listed but was not written by or to TR; not entered under letters.

headline: Jack Elliott comes to stay
summary: Roosevelt's good friend Jack Elliott arrives at Oyster Bay for a visit of five or six weeks.

events.detail: Jack Elliott arrives for an extended stay

tr_quotes.text: Dear old Jack Elliott arrived today, to stay five or six weeks.

headline: Sail, oar and paddle to Lloyd Neck
summary: With a following wind, Roosevelt and Jack Elliott make good time to Lloyd Neck using sail, oars and paddle together. They hunt the lagoons, lunch, fight their way out of the marsh at dead low tide and row home into a headwind, with two yellowlegs and two herons.

events.detail: Hunts the Lloyd Neck lagoons with Jack Elliott
Rows home against a headwind

headline: Six months gone, a glorious sail
summary: Roosevelt and Jack sail in a near-reefing breeze without shortening canvas. He calls Oyster Bay the ideal place for young men and wonders if anyone could be happier, while noting it has been six months since his father died.

events.detail: Sails with Jack Elliott in a stiff breeze
Marks six months since his father's death

tr_quotes.text: Oyster Bay is the perfection of a place for fellows; I often wonder if any one could have a happier time than I am having.
Six months ago
it seems so much longer.

headline: Harvard grades arrive
summary: Roosevelt's Harvard rank list comes, showing an average near 85, a ten-point gain over the year before, with his best marks in German and natural history. He is pleased and thinks his father would have been too, though he is laid up with cholera morbus.

events.detail: Receives his sophomore marks from Harvard, averaging about 85
Laid up with cholera morbus

tr_quotes.text: I am well satisfied; + and my dearest Father would have been so pleased.
Funnily enough I am rather laid up by an attack of cholera morbus.

headline: Missing church, thinking of Father
summary: Still ill, Roosevelt misses church for nearly the first time that year. With idle hours, a rarity for him, his thoughts keep returning to his father.

events.detail: Stays home from church while sick
Spends the idle day thinking of his father

tr_quotes.text: As usual when I have nothing to do (a rare event, thank fortune) I have been thinking a great deal of Father.

headline: Mosquito portage and a note from Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row to Plum Point, haul the boat 200 yards over miserable, mosquito-thick ground into the big marsh behind Centre Island, then hunt, lunch and sail home. Edith Carow has sent a sweet thank-you for her birthday gift.

events.detail: Marsh expedition with Jack Elliott; one sand snipe
Receives a thank-you note from Edith Carow

headline: Riding the tide through Lloyd Neck marsh
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row to Lloyd Neck, going into the marsh as the tide rises and coming out as it falls. A stiff southerly holds them out until late afternoon. One yellowlegs, one sand snipe.

events.detail: Shoots through the Lloyd Neck marsh with Jack Elliott

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Nine hours after woodcock
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock from eight to five without stopping to eat or rest, testing new knickerbockers, gaiters and hunting shoes. The cover is so thick he misses two shots in three, yet he takes six birds and feels completely fresh.

events.detail: Nine-hour woodcock hunt, killing six birds

tr_quotes.text: I tried my new knickerbockers gaiters and hunting shoes, which worked to a charm.
had glorious sport, +, funnily enough, feel fresh as a lark.

headline: Edith visits; caught in a squall
summary: Edith Carow arrives for a two-week stay with Corinne. Roosevelt, Emlen and Jack sail to the Connecticut shore and run into a heavy rainstorm on the way back.

events.detail: Edith Carow arrives to visit Corinne for two weeks
Sails to Connecticut with Emlen and Jack Elliott

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Picnic sail and boxing lessons
summary: Roosevelt, Edith, Corinne, Jack and Emlen sail out for a picnic lunch at Yellowbanks. He starts teaching Jack to box, gets the better of Emlen in a bout, and loses to him at the rifle.

events.detail: Sailing picnic at Yellowbanks
Teaches Jack Elliott to spar and boxes Emlen
Emlen beats him at rifle shooting

headline: Rowing Edith; West's confession
summary: Roosevelt rows Edith out toward Lloyd Neck and spars with Jack and West. Riding with West, he hears all about his cousin's devotion to a young woman named Fanny and is touched by how smitten West is.

events.detail: Rows Edith out toward Lloyd Neck
Spars with Jack Elliott and West
West confides his love for Fanny on a ride

tr_quotes.text: It is really touching to see how much in love he is.

headline: Water lilies with Edith
summary: Roosevelt drives Edith to Cold Spring to gather water lilies, a lovely morning together. In the afternoon Elliott sails in on the Waterwitch with cousin Jack Roosevelt after a three-week cruise.

events.detail: Drives Edith to Cold Spring to pick water lilies
Elliott returns aboard the Waterwitch with Jack Roosevelt

tr_quotes.text: spending a lovely morning with her.

uncertain: 'Coldspring' taken as Cold Spring Harbor; 'Nell' is Elliott.

headline: Family sail and tea at West's
summary: Roosevelt, Elliott and Jack take their mother, Edith and Corinne sailing. That evening a large family party has tea at West's, after which Roosevelt and Edith walk up to the summer house. He worries his hard ride that day may have hurt his horse.

events.detail: Takes Mother, Edith and Corinne sailing with Elliott and Jack
Tea at West's with relatives and cousins
Goes up to the summer house with Edith

tr_quotes.text: My ride today was so long and hard that I am afraid it may have injured my horse.

uncertain: 'Jack' assumed to be Jack Elliott.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Shooting a troublesome dog
summary: Having warned a dog's owner after the animal harassed him on horseback, Roosevelt carries out the threat while riding with West, killing it with his revolver as it runs beside his horse.

events.detail: Shoots a dog that had bothered him on rides

tr_quotes.text: rolling it over with my revolver very neatly as it ran alongside the horse.

headline: Sunday family prayers
summary: Roosevelt notes how much he values the family habit of morning and evening prayers on Sundays.

events.detail: Family prayers morning and evening

tr_quotes.text: I like our custom of having family prayers in the morning and evening of Sunday very much.

headline: A dawn gallop, then off on the Addie
summary: On a crisp, clear morning Roosevelt rides twenty miles at a gallop with Emlen. Around noon he, Emlen, West and Jack board the Addie for a short cruise, reaching New Haven about ten that night in light air.

events.detail: Twenty-mile gallop with Emlen
Sets out on a yachting cruise aboard the Addie
Reaches New Haven around 10 p.m.

headline: Lazy day under sail to New London
summary: Light winds keep the Addie under way until 8 p.m. before she reaches New London. The young men swim, read the New Symposium, climb the rigging and play whist.

events.detail: Sails from New Haven to New London
Reads the New Symposium aboard
Swimming, climbing the rigging and whist

tr_quotes.text: It is very lazy but very pleasant.

headline: Revolver practice off Greenport
summary: The party sails on to Greenport in fitful breezes. With hundreds of cartridges aboard, they fire their revolvers at anything that surfaces, from bottles and buoys to sharks and porpoises.

events.detail: Sails to Greenport
Revolver target practice from the yacht

tr_quotes.text: I never slept or ate better in my life.

headline: Along the Long Island shore
summary: In a steady breeze the Addie sails all day along Long Island's low, sandy shoreline. Roosevelt spends long stretches up in the crosstrees; the rest goes to whist and arguments about materialism and politics.

events.detail: Sails west along the Long Island coast
Whist and debates on materialism and politics

tr_quotes.text: I passed a good deal of time in the cross trees

headline: Cruise ends at Oyster Bay
summary: The Addie reaches Oyster Bay at 1 a.m. and the crew comes ashore for breakfast. Roosevelt has loved the cruise, and in the afternoon he goes sailing again with Jack and Alfred. Corinne writes Edith that her visit was worth another painful goodbye.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay from the cruise
Afternoon sail with Jack Elliott and Alfred
Corinne writes to Edith Carow

tr_quotes.text: Have most heartily enjoyed the cruise,

uncertain: Corinne's letter to Edith is not TR's correspondence; noted as an event only.

headline: Hunting sea coots in vain
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row nearly twenty miles after sea coots without seeing a single one. George Minot arrives for a few days' visit.

events.detail: Rows almost 20 miles after sea coots, finding none
George Minot arrives to stay

headline: Uncertain about the future
summary: Roosevelt talks with Uncle Jim about what he will do with his life and admits he has no idea what follows college. Missing his father's guidance keenly, he decides his job for the next two years is plain: study hard and live as a brave Christian gentleman.

events.detail: Discusses his future at length with Uncle Jim
Grieves for his father's counsel

tr_quotes.text: I have absolutely no idea what I should do when I leave college.
my duty is clear - to study well and live like a brave Christian gentleman.

uncertain: 'Uncle Jim' taken as James King Gracie.

headline: Racing to Rye and back
summary: A strong westerly sends two boats across to Rye and back: Roosevelt and Alfred in the Meteor, with Elliott, Jack and George Minot crewing the Daphne. They lunch with the Bulkleys, where Roosevelt meets Miss Lee Berry.

events.detail: Sails the Meteor to Rye with Alfred
Lunch at the Bulkleys', meeting Miss Lee Berry

headline: Racing a squall to Rocky Point
summary: Roosevelt and Jack plan a night out in the skiff, but heavy rain sends them home. After lunch at Matinecock Point a fierce northwest squall hits off Oak Bluff, and they run before it under sail to Rocky Point, taking on a lot of water.

events.detail: Skiff trip with Jack Elliott, lunching at Matinecock Point
Caught in a heavy squall and runs for Rocky Point

tr_quotes.text: staunch though the little boat is, we shipped a good deal of water.

headline: Grim news about Hal Minot
summary: George Minot tells Roosevelt that his brother Hal, a close friend, has lost his reason and been placed in an asylum. Roosevelt grieves for the gentle, bright young man and his family. Later Uncle Hill and Aunt Susie come to stay.

events.detail: Learns his friend Hal Minot has been committed to an asylum
Uncle Hill and Aunt Susie arrive

tr_quotes.text: he is as sweet and gentle a fellow as I have ever seen, and very bright; and a true friend to me

uncertain: Two words in the diary are illegible in the source.

headline: Sad news, then dinner at the Union League
summary: Overnighting in New York, Roosevelt visits Cassin, who is slowly dying, and learns that Cousin Sam Roosevelt has died. Still low about Hal Minot, he dines that evening at the Union League Club with Jack Roosevelt and Emlen.

events.detail: Goes into New York for the night
Visits his dying friend Cassin
Learns of Cousin Sam Roosevelt's death
Dines at the Union League Club with Jack Roosevelt and Emlen

tr_quotes.text: Called on poor Cassin; he is dying by inches.

headline: Northbound for the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt, West and Emlen board an early-morning train to Boston, bound for three weeks in the Maine woods. Writing of Hal Minot, he says his father's death has dulled his ability to grieve.

events.detail: Takes the morning train to Boston with West and Emlen

tr_quotes.text: Father's death has taken away much of my capacity for grieving.

headline: Arriving at Island Falls
summary: After an overnight train to Mattawamkeag, the party rides a buckboard to Island Falls, arriving at 8 p.m. Roosevelt is suffering a bad bout of asthma and misses his horse.

events.detail: Overnight train to Mattawamkeag, then buckboard to Island Falls
Has a bad attack of asthma

tr_quotes.text: Have a pretty bad attack of asthma

uncertain: Source has 'Highland Island Falls'; read as Island Falls.

headline: Psalm 19 and a Methodist meeting
summary: Roosevelt walks, reads his Bible and memorizes Psalm 19. With no church in Island Falls, he attends a Methodist meeting in the schoolhouse. Thoughts of Hal Minot bring back his grief for his father.

events.detail: Learns Psalm 19 by heart
Attends a Methodist meeting in the schoolhouse

tr_quotes.text: I try whenever I can only to recall his grand and beautful life. Oh Father, Father!

headline: Partridge hunt, seven months on
summary: Seven months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the whole day after partridges without seeing one.

events.detail: Hunts partridges all day without sighting any

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day hunting partridges but did not even see one.

headline: Paddling down to Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: The party heads downstream to camp at the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake, the others in a bateau with guide Sewall while Roosevelt goes ahead by canoe with guide Dow. He enjoys the paddling and woods walking but misses every shot at pigeons and ducks.

events.detail: Canoes downstream to Mattawamkeag Lake with guide Dow
Several misses at pigeons and ducks
Sets up camp at the foot of the lake

tr_quotes.text: I had good fun paddling, and tramping through the woods

uncertain: 'Will T.' identified as Will Thompson from the 9/23 'Thornson'; guides taken as Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow.

headline: A loon at long range and a quiet ramble
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen canoe the lake; Roosevelt fires at a loon over a hundred yards away and nearly hits it. In the afternoon they hike about ten miles after partridge, taking one ruffed grouse, and he praises Emlen as a loyal companion.

events.detail: Rifle shots at a distant loon from the canoe
Ten-mile woods walk after partridge; one ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: he and I are great companions and he is a true friend.

headline: Rainy day in camp
summary: Rain keeps the party under canvas with books, cards and gun cleaning, eating duck, partridge, trout and pickerel. Roosevelt and Emlen sit three hours in the wet waiting for ducks and come back empty-handed.

events.detail: Rainy day in camp with cards and gun cleaning
Waits in a blind for ducks with Emlen; no luck

headline: Still raining at camp
summary: Another wet day of reading, euchre, whist and rifle practice in camp. Roosevelt waits for ducks again with one long miss, and kills a bat and a nighthawk.

events.detail: Stays in camp, playing cards and shooting at targets
Kills a bat and a nighthawk

tr_quotes.text: I killed a bat and a nighthawk.

headline: Missing foxes across the river
summary: When the rain stops at noon, Roosevelt hikes fifteen miles with Sewall and comes back with nothing. He misses two foxes at about sixty yards and is fed up with his week of poor shooting.

events.detail: Fifteen-mile hunt with Sewall; misses two foxes

tr_quotes.text: I am disgusted with myself.

headline: Bible, guns and specimens
summary: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then fills the afternoon cleaning guns and labeling specimens before a swim in the mill race.

events.detail: Morning Bible reading
Labels specimens
Bathes in the mill race

tr_quotes.text: Read my bible in the morning

headline: Thirty miles along the Mattawamkeag
summary: After a frosty night, Roosevelt and Sewall hike thirty miles near the Mattawamkeag River, on the move from eight to seven save a half-hour lunch. He gets only four shots, bagging a rabbit, a merganser and two grouse, but loves the walk.

events.detail: Thirty-mile hunting tramp with Sewall

tr_quotes.text: But enjoyed the walk greatly.

headline: A night in a wigwam
summary: Roosevelt, West and guide Dow paddle to the head of the lake and hunt the sloughs and bogs with middling luck, taking two ducks. The three camp overnight in a wigwam on a meager supper.

events.detail: Hunts the bogs at the head of the lake by canoe
Camps out in a wigwam

headline: Up at four for ducks
summary: Up before dawn, the three hunt ducks and see none. Back at the main camp, Roosevelt walks about ten miles with Will Dow for four shots, a merganser and three grouse, and decides moccasins are the best footwear for the woods.

events.detail: Pre-dawn duck hunt, unsuccessful
Ten-mile hunt with Will Dow

tr_quotes.text: I like moccasins to walk through the woods with very much.

headline: Through alder and cedar swamps
summary: Roosevelt hikes about fifteen miles, three of them through some of the hardest swamp walking he has known. He takes a spruce partridge among the cedars and a ruffed grouse up on a hemlock ridge.

events.detail: Fifteen-mile hike through swamps, shooting partridges
Takes a spruce grouse and a ruffed grouse

headline: Fooled by a decoy duck
summary: On a ten-mile walk with Sewall, Roosevelt stalks and kills a duck on a small lake. The others then trick him with a dead duck propped up to look alive in a pond. He has bathed in the mill race daily.

events.detail: Stalks and shoots a duck with Sewall
Falls for a prank with a propped-up dead duck

tr_quotes.text: Was nicely sold by the boys with a dead duck placed in a life like attitude in a pond.

headline: Autumn color in the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen hunt in the afternoon; Emlen never fires, and Roosevelt misses a duck but drops a partridge. The leaves are turning, and he counts the trip a real success.

events.detail: Afternoon hunt with Emlen; one ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: The leaves are now beginning to turn and the woods are perfectly beautiful.

headline: Quiet Sunday in camp
summary: Roosevelt passes Sunday much as he did the week before.

events.detail: A quiet Sunday in camp

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day much as last Sunday.

headline: Breaking camp by bateau
summary: The party breaks camp and heads back to Island Falls in the clumsy bateau: Sewall paddling, Roosevelt and Dow at the oars, Thompson trolling, and West and Emlen in the bow watching for game. Roosevelt spends the afternoon in the woods with West.

events.detail: Returns to Island Falls by bateau
Afternoon woods walk with West; one ruffed grouse

uncertain: 'Thornson' read as Thompson.

headline: Twenty-five miles with Dow
summary: Roosevelt hikes 25 miles with Dow, taking a woodcock and two partridges. Game has been scarce all trip, but he has loved it, and the party has not had one quarrel.

events.detail: Twenty-five-mile hunt with Dow

tr_quotes.text: There has been absolutely no disagreement between any members of the party.

uncertain: 'log cock' likely a woodcock.

headline: Hunting from a buckboard
summary: Roosevelt rides around all day in a buckboard, Will Dow at his side, climbing down each time they spot a partridge. He gets five grouse and sees a fox.

events.detail: Drives the roads with Dow, stopping for partridges; five grouse
Sees a fox

headline: Leaving Maine
summary: The party drives by wagon to Mattawamkeag and boards the night train for Boston. His companions will continue to New York; Roosevelt is bound back to Harvard.

events.detail: Wagon to Mattawamkeag and night train for Boston

headline: Back at Harvard, a surprise invitation
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge for his junior year to a warm welcome. To his astonishment the Porcellian Club asks him to join, and he feels he must decline because he belongs to the A.D. Club, though he wishes otherwise. His sister Corinne turns 17.

events.detail: Returns to Harvard for his junior year
Offered membership in the Porcellian Club
Corinne's 17th birthday

tr_quotes.text: To my great surprise I was offered the Porcellian; of course I could not accept, being a member of the A.D. - but I wish I could.

headline: Settling into the junior-year routine
summary: Roosevelt finds his classes and lab work will fill about twenty hours a week, with an 8 a.m. recitation daily, Saturdays included. Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall each invite him for Sunday, and his club table at Mrs. Wilson's serves excellent meals.

events.detail: Sizes up a schedule of about 20 class hours a week
Invitations from Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall

headline: Sunday church in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt goes to church and plans to resume teaching Sunday school in a week or two.

events.detail: Attends church

tr_quotes.text: I shall not take up my sunday school till next Sunday or the one after.

headline: Down to work and the rifle club
summary: Roosevelt starts studying in earnest and joins the rifle club, meaning to shoot regularly this year. In New York the cables for the Brooklyn Bridge are finished.

events.detail: Begins his regular course of study
Joins the Harvard rifle club
Cable-spinning on the Brooklyn Bridge is completed

tr_quotes.text: I joined the rifle club; I am going to practice pretty regularly with the rifle this year.

headline: Into the Glee Club
summary: Roosevelt is voted into the Harvard Glee Club.

events.detail: Elected to the Glee Club

tr_quotes.text: Was elected into the Glee club.

headline: At the D.K.E., but not drinking
summary: Roosevelt attends the first D.K.E. meeting of the year. He finds its drinking tiresome as a steady diet, though fun now and then; he does not drink there, drinks very little anyway, and will not smoke before he is 21.

events.detail: Attends the first D.K.E. meeting of the year

tr_quotes.text: I shall not begin smoking till I am twenty one; as it is, I drink very little.

headline: First meeting of the Art Club
summary: Roosevelt goes to the opening meeting of the Art Club and enjoys it.

events.detail: Attends the Art Club's first meeting

tr_quotes.text: Attended the first meeting of the Art Club, and found it very pleasant.

headline: Favorite courses: philosophy and economics
summary: Roosevelt ranks his courses: philosophy and political economy come first, natural history is engaging if less so than last year, and the rest interest him little.

events.detail: Reflects on which of his courses he likes best

tr_quotes.text: Of my studies this year I like best the philosophy and political economy

headline: Morning at the rifle range
summary: Roosevelt spends the morning shooting at the range.

events.detail: Morning of rifle practice

tr_quotes.text: Spent the morning at the rifle range.

headline: Communion Sunday at Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt marks Communion Sunday.

events.detail: Observes Communion Sunday

tr_quotes.text: Communion Sunday

headline: Hard work, with holidays ahead
summary: Roosevelt is studying hard, but his strong average last year earns him optional recitations, so he expects some three weeks of winter holidays.

events.detail: Works hard; optional recitations promise winter time off

tr_quotes.text: I am working pretty hard now

headline: Boxing lessons resume
summary: Roosevelt starts up again with his boxing teacher and writes his mother an affectionate letter saying his studies take six or seven hours a day.

events.detail: Resumes lessons with his boxing teacher
Writes to his mother about his studies

letters.topic: Affectionate note reporting six or seven hours of study daily

tr_quotes.text: Darling, beloved, little motherling

headline: Caught between two clubs
summary: After two drunk club men argue about him and reveal his preference for the Porcellian, the A.D. members vote to let Roosevelt choose between the clubs, since he never formally joined theirs. Knowing either choice will hurt someone, he spends a miserable day weighing what honor requires.

events.detail: The A.D. Club offers to release him to choose the Porcellian

headline: A winter sleigh ride to Island Falls
summary: Bill Sewall meets Roosevelt's train at Mattawamkeag with a sleigh, and the two travel 36 miles over half-broken roads, reaching Island Falls near ten at night. The air is bitter but still, and well bundled, Roosevelt loves the ride. Elliott turns 19. His notes on Oyster Bay birds are dated to this period.

events.detail: Met by Bill Sewall at Mattawamkeag
36-mile sleigh ride to Island Falls
Elliott's 19th birthday
His early checklist of Oyster Bay bird life

tr_quotes.text: It was bitterly cold, but still, and we were well wrapped up, so I enjoyed the ride very much,

works.title: Notes on Some of the Birds of Oyster Bay, Long Island

references.title: Theodore Roosevelt Association Journal, "Twin Literary Rarities of T.R." by Paul Russell Cutright

uncertain: The bird-notes title and Cutright citation appear appended to this date; its exact publication date is unclear.

headline: First try on snowshoes in Maine
summary: Roosevelt straps on snowshoes for the first time and covers about six miles checking lynx traps with Will Dow. The traps are empty, but he marvels at the snow-heavy evergreens and drops a porcupine from a hemlock with his rifle.

events.detail: Learns to snowshoe on a six-mile circuit of lynx traps
Shoots a porcupine out of a hemlock with his rifle
Notes tracks of lynx, foxes, otters and rabbits

tr_quotes.text: Tried snowshoing for the first time. Went about six miles, making the round of Will Dow's "lucivee' [lynx] traps, which however contained nothing. The woods looked simply perfect, all the evergreens being loaded with snow; I have never seen a grander sight than these northern forests in winter. I got along very well, except in a cedar swamp. We saw many tracks of lucivees, foxes, otters and rabbits; and found a porcupine up in a hemlock. I brought him down quite neatly with the rifle.

uncertain: 'lucivee' is a Maine word for lynx; 'Will Dow' taken as Wilmot Dow.

headline: Bible reading and a winter tramp
summary: A quiet Sunday: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then walks the snowy pine and spruce woods in the afternoon. He finds the cold easy to bear among the trees but harsh in the wind, and notes how little life stirs in the forest.

events.detail: Reads his Bible in the morning
Afternoon snowshoe walk through pine and spruce forest

tr_quotes.text: Read my bible in the morning. In the afternoon took a tramp through the woods; I can not get used to the extreme beauty of the snow covered pine and spruce forests. The cold does not bother me at all in the woods, but if there is any wind it is very disagreeable in the open. I get along very well on snow shoes, but the swamps are very tough work - although perhaps not so bad as in summer. There is very little life in the woods.

headline: Eight hours in the woods with Dow
summary: With Will Dow, Roosevelt hikes to Dyer Brook and then strikes off cross-country through hardwoods and tangled spruce and cedar swamps. Over an eight-hour tramp he logs an arctic woodpecker, chickadees, two gray jays at lunch, and the tracks of hare, lynx and spruce grouse.

events.detail: Long winter hike to Dyer Brook and through the woods
Records an arctic woodpecker, chickadees, whiskey jacks and lynx tracks

tr_quotes.text: Went off on a tramp through the woods with Will Dow. Walked up to Dyer Brook, then a couple of miles along it, and then struck out in the woods. The best walking was on the hard wood grounds; it was fearfully hard work in some of the thick, swampy spruce and cedar thickets, but not as bad as in summer. I saw an arctic woodpecker by a stream and some Halldronian chickadees in a spruce wood, and two whiskey jacks came round us at lunch time; we saw two or three hare tracks, and once the round footprints of a canada lynx, and found where a spruce partridge had passed the night; but in an 8 hour tramp, these were the only traces of life.

uncertain: 'Halldronian chickadees' is as written in the source, likely Hudsonian chickadees.

headline: A ruffed grouse after a long hunt
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in the woods with Bill Sewall. Tracks of a dozen kinds of animals are everywhere, yet they see only chickadees and a woodpecker until they trail a partridge, flush it from a fallen birch and Roosevelt brings it down.

events.detail: Tracks and shoots a ruffed grouse with Sewall
Notes tracks of lynx, mink, weasel, otter and porcupine

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day tramping through the woods with Will Seawall. We saw a good many tracks of lucivees, foxes, rabbits, otters, minks, weasels, squirrels, porcupines + c; but the only living creatures were a couple of chickadees and a woodpecker. Finally we found the footprints of a partridge on some hardwood ground, and following them up roused the bird from under a fallen birch top, and I shot it. The snow shoing [sic] is poor, the snow being wet or heavy, and the weather warmish. 1 ruffed grouse.

uncertain: 'Will Seawall' taken as William Wingate Sewall.

headline: Asthma at night, grouse by day
summary: Another day of snowshoeing with little game to show for it, though Roosevelt is having the time of his life. Asthma keeps him awake at night. After lunch at a logging camp he shoots a partridge from a spruce top and a porcupine; the traps have so far yielded a lynx and a fox.

events.detail: Snowshoes through the woods all day
Asthma disturbs his sleep
Shoots a partridge and a porcupine; traps hold a lynx and a fox

tr_quotes.text: Otherwise I am enjoying myself to the utmost, but the asthma keeps me up a good deal at night.

headline: Thirty miles by pung to a logging camp
summary: Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow set out with a box sleigh and a scrawny horse for a logging camp thirty miles off, arriving after dark. It is ten below at the start and the roads are terrible. Along the way he spots a red crossbill, flocks of snow buntings and some unusually tame grosbeaks.

events.detail: Rides a pung sleigh thirty miles to a logging camp
Sees snow buntings, a red crossbill, grosbeaks and mouse tracks

tr_quotes.text: When we started the thermometer was 10° below zero, but I was too well wrapped up to heed the cold

headline: On the trail of a caribou
summary: Through a heavy snowstorm Roosevelt and Dow hunt all day, finally jumping a caribou in thick spruce. He glimpses it at under thirty yards but cannot shoot, and they track it until dark, then spend a cold, hungry night by a big fire with no blankets.

events.detail: Startles a caribou and follows its tracks until dusk
Camps overnight in the snow with little food and no blankets

tr_quotes.text: I caught a glimpse of him as he vanished not thirty yards distant, but had no chance to fire.

headline: Caribou chase ends without a shot
summary: Before sunrise, in subzero cold, the hunters take up the caribou's trail again through swamps, ledges and open cranberry bogs. Roosevelt studies how the animal trots and bounds in snow over three feet deep. By midday they quit and are back at the logging camp at sunset.

events.detail: Follows the caribou until midday, then gives up
Observes how a caribou moves through deep snow

tr_quotes.text: Generally he trotted, coming down not only on his hoofs but on his whole lower legs, the snow being over three feet deep, but in bad ground he made great jumps like a huge rabbit.

headline: Resting among the lumbermen
summary: Worn out from two days after the caribou, Roosevelt rests. His asthma has not troubled him since reaching camp, and he warms to the rough, generous lumbermen, especially one named Charley Brown. Rain followed by frost has coated every tree in ice.

events.detail: Rests at the logging camp after the caribou hunt
Befriends the lumbermen, especially Charley Brown

tr_quotes.text: I like these lumbermen very much, and get on capitally with them - great, rough, hospitable fellows. I am great friends with one in especial, Charley Brown.

headline: A buck, rabbits and a venison feast
summary: Roosevelt and Sewall find a small deer yard. He trips and misses his first shot at the buck, then runs it down over a mile and kills it with his rifle. After an afternoon of rabbit hunting, venison replaces the usual pork and beans. He writes his mother that he has stored up health enough to last into summer.

events.detail: Kills a buck after a mile-long chase
Shoots three white rabbits with the rifle
Writes to his mother about his improved health

letters.topic: His health is restored by the Maine trip

tr_quotes.text: In the evening we had a royal venison supper - a pleasant change from the ordinary routine of pork + beans.
I have got enough health to last me till next summer.

headline: Dragging the sleigh back to Island Falls
summary: The return trip is miserable: sleet and rain, wretched roads, and a horse that keeps floundering into drifts until the men unhitch it and haul the sleigh themselves. Wet, chilled and hungry after walking the whole way, Roosevelt still notes snow buntings singing, and reaches Island Falls by teatime.

events.detail: Returns by sleigh from the logging camp to Island Falls
Hears snow buntings singing

tr_quotes.text: Several times when the horse floundered off the track into the deep snow drifts we had to unharness him and drag the sleigh ourselves for a hundred yards or so.

headline: A raccoon and a camp on Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: After another empty seven-mile trap round, Roosevelt follows a raccoon's track and shoots it from a dead tree. The party then snowshoes to Mattawamkeag Lake and camps at its foot, picking up two spruce grouse on the way in the best snow conditions of his stay.

events.detail: Tracks and shoots a raccoon
Snowshoes to Mattawamkeag Lake and camps
Shoots two spruce grouse in a swamp

tr_quotes.text: The snowshoing, for the first time since I have been up here, was capital.

uncertain: Source spells the lake 'Mattawomkeag'.

headline: Long-range rifle practice on the ice
summary: The party breaks camp and returns to Island Falls by dinner, traveling over the frozen lake and river. Seeing no game, they pass the time shooting at targets 300 to 500 yards off, and all three do well with a Sharps rifle.

events.detail: Returns to Island Falls over the frozen lake and river
Target shooting at 300 to 500 yards with a Sharps rifle

tr_quotes.text: I enjoyed the walk extremely.

headline: Counting trophies from two happy weeks
summary: A last morning hunt turns up no partridges and empty traps, but Roosevelt is content. He sums up the trip as his pleasantest two weeks ever, with skins of fox, lynx, raccoon and buck to take home, plenty of game eaten and many specimens collected.

events.detail: Final partridge hunt and trap round, both empty
Takes stock of skins and specimens collected

tr_quotes.text: However I have had good success this trip, and I have never passed a pleasanter two weeks. The skins of the fox, lucivee [lynx], coon and buck make quite a set of trophies;

uncertain: Source also quotes Bill Sewall's later recollection of TR on this trip (from Morris); not reproduced.

headline: Leaving Maine to catch up on studies
summary: Roosevelt leaves by sleigh at five in the morning for Mattawamkeag and boards the night train to Boston. He resolves to work double time until Easter to make up for the holiday.

events.detail: Sleigh ride to Mattawamkeag at dawn
Night train toward Boston

tr_quotes.text: I am now going to study all the time till Easter, doing double work to make up for my holiday.

tr_quotes.text: Got home this morning at 11 o'clock, too late for church.

tr_quotes.text: Am teaching my horse to trot, as I think of putting him in a tilbury next winter.

With the tide and no wind, the outward leg takes under three hours; the return, into a stiff headwind, takes four and a half and ships plenty of water. Charades and dancing follow at the crowded house.

events.detail: Rows to Sheffield Island lighthouse and back
Evening of dancing and charades with houseguests

tr_quotes.text: Rowed across the sound to Sheffield Island light and back, a distance of 30 miles.

headline: Setting out on the Meteor
summary: Roosevelt, Alfred and West set off for a week aboard the Meteor, an open 24-foot sloop, stocked with hardtack, canned meat and coffee. The breeze dies by evening and they anchor off the Saugatuck River, sleeping in sailors' hammocks slung in the cockpit.

events.detail: Begins a week's cruise aboard the Meteor
Drops anchor where the Saugatuck River meets the Sound

tr_quotes.text: This trip we have sailors hammocks , which we sling in the cock pit - great improvment to our former way of sleeping on the boards.

headline: Sheltering at the Thimble Islands
summary: The Meteor weighs anchor at 5:30 into light headwinds. Roosevelt notes terns, gulls, coots and a storm petrel. Becalmed in the afternoon, they anchor off the Thimble Islands, then run for shelter behind one when a southerly wind kicks up at night.

events.detail: Sails east along the Connecticut shore
Sees terns, gulls, coots and a stormy petrel
Anchors at the Thimble Islands and shelters from a night wind

tr_quotes.text: I saw a good many terns and gulls and a few coots - also a stormy petrel.

headline: A rough beat to New London
summary: Low on water, the crew sails on Sunday despite Roosevelt's misgivings. Beating into a strengthening northeaster and a heavy sea, they struggle off Bartlett's Reef to keep the boat upright, taking on much water, and reach New London at 4 p.m.

events.detail: Beats into a northeast gale and reaches New London

tr_quotes.text: I don't like sailing on Sunday but we are short of water + must reach New London.

headline: Dinner with the Chapins, revolvers at sea
summary: The sailors call at the Chapins' house for dinner, then turn back into a strong southwesterly and put into Saybrook at sunset. Sharks and porpoises along the way serve as revolver targets.

events.detail: Dines at the Chapin family's house
Sails west and anchors at Saybrook
Takes revolver shots at sharks and porpoises

tr_quotes.text: Saw a shark or two and a good many porpoises

headline: Fighting out of Saybrook
summary: Leaving at 5 a.m., the Meteor battles over the shoals and tide rips at Saybrook's harbor mouth in a strong wind and big sea. Rain falls all morning, the breeze dies at noon, and they anchor in the lee of Charles Island at 7:30.

events.detail: Crosses the Saybrook shoals and sails to Charles Island

tr_quotes.text: At 7.30 we came to anchor under the lee of Charles Island.

headline: Rowing home in a dead calm
summary: Light, shifting winds give way to a flat calm from nine to six, and the crew labors at the long oars, not reaching Oyster Bay until 11:15 that night. Roosevelt judges the cruise a great success and his cousins fine company.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay, much of the way under oars

tr_quotes.text: Al and Doc are not only good friends but extremely pleasant companions.
The trip has been a great success.

Evenings mean reading, whist or dancing, and he often takes Miss Hale of Philadelphia, a guest of Aunt Lizzie's, out rowing.

summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock with young Pendleton Cruger from seven in the morning to seven at night through brutal cover in the heat, wading waist-deep in mud holes and swamps. Cruger shoots well; Roosevelt says he does not. They bag seven birds.

events.detail: Day-long woodcock hunt with Pendleton Cruger; seven birds

tr_quotes.text: He is a pretty good shot - I am not.

summary: Hunting with Cruger again, Roosevelt works Fleet's swamp, Townsend's and the Beekman place, then a string of boggy spots near Locust Valley. For once, he notes, he shoots very well.

summary: Roosevelt counts Emily Swan among the prettiest and most charming young women in Oyster Bay, and has enjoyed several rows and rides with her.

headline: Junior grades top the class in zoology
summary: Roosevelt's junior-year marks arrive: an average above 87 percent, his best yet, and first in the class in zoology and political economy. Afternoons bring tennis and a swim with Elliott, and the horse is getting used to harness.

events.detail: Receives junior-year marks, averaging over 87 percent
Lawn tennis and swimming with Elliott

tr_quotes.text: In Zoology and Political Economy I lead every body.

headline: A happy home
summary: Roosevelt notes the family's Sunday morning and evening prayers and wishes they were daily. He writes warmly of his mother, his sisters Bamie and Corinne, and Elliott, his best friend, who together make as happy a home as anyone could ask for.

events.detail: Sunday morning and evening family prayers

tr_quotes.text: Every Sunday we have morning, and evening prayers; I wish we could have them every day.
These three, and my best friend, old brother Nell, give me as happy a home as a man could possibly have.

headline: Weighing science or law
summary: On the eve of leaving for Maine, Roosevelt reflects on a fine, sunburned summer. He is thinking hard about life after college and expects either to pursue science or to read law as a path into public life.

events.detail: Prepares to leave for the Maine woods
Considers a scientific career or law study leading to public life

tr_quotes.text: am thinking pretty seriously as to what I shall do when I leave College; I shall probably either pursue a scientific course, or else study law, preparatory to going into public life.

headline: Dinner at the University Club
summary: In New York Roosevelt praises his guardians, Uncle Jim Roosevelt and Uncle Jimmie Gracie, as the best he could have. That evening Douglas Robinson joins him for dinner at the University Club, along with Haddon, Stratton, Sedgwick and Kingsford.

events.detail: Goes from Oyster Bay into New York
Meets with his guardians
Dinner at the University Club

tr_quotes.text: I wonder if there could be two better guardians than Uncle Jim Roosevelt and Uncle Jimmie Gracie! I can't imagine it.

uncertain: 'Uncle Jim Roosevelt' taken as James A. Roosevelt; 'Haddon' assumed Harold Haddon.

headline: Warm welcome at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt travels to Boston and on to Chestnut Hill, where Dick Saltonstall greets him heartily. After dining with Mrs. Lee they drive to the Whitneys', where Bessie, Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice are staying, and plan a picnic for Ell Whitney's birthday.

events.detail: Travels to Boston and Chestnut Hill
Dines with Mrs. Lee, then visits the Whitneys

tr_quotes.text: dear old Dick gave me the most hearty and enthusiastic greeting.

headline: Picnic day at the Whitneys'
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive to the Whitneys' at nine and stay past midnight, sailing, walking, dancing and playing tennis. He is especially glad to see Rose and Alice again.

events.detail: Birthday outing at the Whitneys' with a large party

tr_quotes.text: The Whitneys are exceedingly hospitable and cordial.

headline: Turning down Alice to keep a promise
summary: Roosevelt visits Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice in town as they leave for the Slades', and they press him to come along. Alice is so lovely that refusing is hard, but he keeps his promise to meet Emlen and takes the night train for Mattawamkeag after dinner with Frank Lee at the Union Club. On the train he writes Bamie about his Boston stay.

events.detail: Sees Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice off to the Slades'
Dines with Frank Lee at the Union Club
Night train for Mattawamkeag, Maine
Letter to Bamie from the train

letters.topic: His Boston visit with Alice and why he left for Maine

tr_quotes.text: Alice was so bewitchingly pretty that it was frightfully hard to refuse.

headline: Back in the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt reaches Mattawamkeag at 10 a.m. and drives to Island Falls with Dave Sewall. Emlen and Arthur Cutler are there, and he plans a short trip with them to Mount Katahdin.

events.detail: Reaches Mattawamkeag and drives to Island Falls
Plans a Katahdin trip with Emlen and Arthur Cutler

tr_quotes.text: I shall make a short trip with them to Katahdin.

uncertain: Source spells the name 'Seawall'.

headline: Packing for Katahdin
summary: Roosevelt spends the day getting ready, listing his kit: two changes of clothes, wool socks, a flannel shirt, duck trousers, a blanket and thick jacket, plus rifle and shotgun.

events.detail: Prepares gear for the Katahdin trip

tr_quotes.text: I have taken both rifle + shot gun.

headline: Paddling the lake with Emlen
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen paddle about 25 miles to their former campsite at the lake's lower end and back. No partridges turn up, but he picks up wood ducks along the channels and praises Emlen and Arthur as good-natured trail partners.

events.detail: Canoes about 25 miles round trip with Emlen
Shoots wood ducks

tr_quotes.text: Em + Arthur are capitel fellows for a trip of this kind -unselfish, good natured, and not minding a little fatigue + hardship.

uncertain: Lake not named; taken as Mattawamkeag Lake from the March trip.

headline: Starting for Katahdin with a 45-pound pack
summary: Roosevelt, Emlen, Arthur Cutler, Will Dow and Bill Sewall set out for Mount Katahdin, driving 23 miles and then backpacking about ten before camping. He carries roughly 45 pounds and loses a shoe in a stream crossing, luckily having moccasins tied to his pack.

events.detail: Sets out for Mount Katahdin by wagon and on foot
Loses a shoe fording a stream; switches to moccasins

tr_quotes.text: I carried about 45 lbs, including my gun + cartridges.

headline: Campfire at Katahdin Lake
summary: The party walks to the upper end of Katahdin Lake and makes camp. Roosevelt stalks and kills four ducks, adds two grouse, and they land some trout. By day the black flies are fierce, but evenings around the blazing fire feel like old times.

events.detail: Treks to the upper end of Katahdin Lake
Kills ducks and grouse; fishes for trout

tr_quotes.text: It is very pleasant + Like old times in the evenings, round the roaring logs of the camp fire.

headline: Lost after dark
summary: After a morning partridge hunt the group heads for Katahdin, catching about a hundred trout at Sandy Brook. Then they lose their way, push through terrible ground into the night, and camp beside a small water hole, soaked, worn out and hungry yet happy. Fresh bear and caribou tracks are everywhere.

events.detail: Morning partridge hunt
Lands roughly a hundred trout in Sandy Brook
Gets lost and camps by a water hole after dark

tr_quotes.text: wet, tired and hungry - but happy.

headline: Climbing Mount Katahdin
summary: Starting before dawn, Roosevelt climbs Mount Katahdin through hard terrain; Emlen and Arthur give out before the top, but he reaches the summit and its fine view. He finds he can bear fatigue nearly as well as the woodsmen. Back at Katahdin Lake by dark, in rain, with about 60 trout.

events.detail: Climbs to the summit of Mount Katahdin
Follows a blazed trail back to camp at Katahdin Lake

tr_quotes.text: I find I can endure fatigue + hardship pretty nearly as well as these lumbermen.

uncertain: Source names Emlen and Arthur as stopping short; the two backwoodsmen are presumably Dow and Sewall.

headline: Scarce game around the lake
summary: Roosevelt circles half the lake in the morning without seeing anything, then walks down Sandy Brook in the afternoon and takes a black duck on Moose Pond. Small trout are plentiful, but game is sparse or out of reach.

events.detail: Hunts around Katahdin Lake and along Sandy Brook
Shoots a black duck on Moose Pond

tr_quotes.text: Trout of small size are very plentiful.

headline: A lazy Sunday in camp
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday around camp cleaning guns, mending clothes and bathing in the lake. The black flies torment his companions but hardly trouble him, and though game is scarce he is having a grand time.

events.detail: Camp chores and a swim in the lake

tr_quotes.text: You get pretty dirty in camp.
but I am enjoying myself exceedingly.

headline: Breaking camp for Island Falls
summary: Up before sunrise, Roosevelt hunts the bogs around a barrens pond and wounds a duck that escapes into the rushes. In the afternoon the party shoulders packs and heads for Island Falls, camping after crossing the Wassataquoik. He says he can now walk, wrestle and shoot with most of the lumbermen.

events.detail: Dawn duck hunt around the bogs
Breaks camp and hikes toward Island Falls, crossing the Wassataquoik

tr_quotes.text: Am in beautiful condition; + I find I can walk, wrestle + shoot with most of these lumbermen.

uncertain: Source spells the stream 'Wissaticock'.

headline: Katahdin trip ends at Island Falls
summary: The party hikes to the Penobscot's East Branch, fords it and rides on to Island Falls. Roosevelt calls the trip a delight and his companions excellent company.

events.detail: Fords the Penobscot's East Branch and returns to Island Falls

tr_quotes.text: I have enjoyed the trip exceedingly; the boys are most pleasant companions.

headline: Buckboard hunt comes up empty
summary: Roosevelt spends the afternoon riding around in a buckboard in search of partridges, without seeing a single bird.

events.detail: Unsuccessful partridge hunt by buckboard

tr_quotes.text: Spent the afternoon driving about in a buckboard looking for partridges; but saw none.

headline: Outfitting a canoe trip with Sewall
summary: Roosevelt prepares for a trip to the Munsungan waters, just he and Bill Sewall in a canoe. He packs tea, pork, hardtack and flour, a shelter tent, two blankets, spare underclothes and plenty of ammunition, and plans to wear only moccasins. He writes Bamie that moccasins served his feet well on Katahdin.

events.detail: Packs for a canoe trip with Sewall
Letter to Bamie about moccasins on the Katahdin climb

letters.topic: How moccasins protected his feet climbing Katahdin

tr_quotes.text: I shall go in a canoe alone with Seawall.
I shall only use moccasins.

uncertain: Spelling of the Munsungan waters varies in the source ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Forty-five miles to the Aroostook Oxbow
summary: Setting off before dawn by farm wagon, Roosevelt and Sewall cover 45 miles of thinly settled forest and some burned-over land to reach the Oxbow of the Aroostook by 6 p.m. They lodge in a bare-bones backwoods house. From the wagon he shoots a spruce grouse and a red-tailed hawk.

events.detail: Wagon journey to the Oxbow of the Aroostook River
Bags a spruce grouse and a red-tailed hawk while riding

tr_quotes.text: fare and sleeping accomodations being both primative to a degree.

headline: Poling up the Aroostook in a dugout
summary: In a dugout that handles rough going better than birchbark, the pair works some twenty miles upriver on the Aroostook, mostly poling. The country is wild and lovely, with no sign of people or game, though trout abound. They camp before dark to cook bread, trout and partridge.

events.detail: Poles a dugout some twenty miles upriver
Camps and cooks trout and partridge

tr_quotes.text: The scenery is very beautiful and wild; I saw no trace of man - but also no trace of game.

headline: Wading the Munsungan in the rain
summary: They push on despite the Sabbath, though Roosevelt neither shoots nor fishes. After poling to the Munsungan's mouth by lunchtime, they wade upstream hauling the boat, sometimes hip-deep, in heavy rain, and camp at dusk soaked and spent.

events.detail: Observes Sunday by not hunting or fishing
Drags the boat up the Munsungan Stream in rain

tr_quotes.text: I compromised by not shooting or fishing.

uncertain: Diary marker OCR'd as [DJ]. Spelling of the Munsungan waters varies in the source ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Beaver dams, falls and a lovely time
summary: In steady rain they drag the heavy dugout through rapids, cut through beaver dams and logjams, unload it to climb past falls, then paddle across the lower Munsungan Lake and halfway up the middle one to camp. Roosevelt is cold, wet and hungry but still enjoying himself, though there is no sign of game.

events.detail: Hauls the dugout upstream and paddles into the Munsungan Lakes

tr_quotes.text: Tired out, + wet through, hungry + cold - but am having a lovely time.

uncertain: Spelling of the Munsungan waters varies in the source ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Turning back for lack of game
summary: Through more rain they paddle up the middle lake and slog over brutal terrain to the top of the upper lake. Roosevelt finds only old moose sign, a fresh bear track, a few grouse, loons and mergansers, so he decides to head back to Island Falls rather than stay as planned.

events.detail: Paddles and hikes to the upper Munsungan Lake
Notes moose and bear tracks, loons and fish ducks
Shoots three ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: although the work is very hard, I am enjoying the trip greatly.

uncertain: Spelling of the Munsungan waters varies in the source ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Running the rapids downstream
summary: Starting before sunrise, Roosevelt and Sewall paddle out of the lakes, run the falls, wade the quick water and then pole swiftly downstream, reaching Saturday's campsite by early afternoon. He treasures the evenings by the fire under their small tent.

events.detail: Descends from the Munsungan Lakes to the Aroostook

tr_quotes.text: I am very fond of the evenings round the camp fire, beneath the little tent.

uncertain: Spelling of the Munsungan waters varies in the source ('Munsingon', 'Munsingan').

headline: Living off the land
summary: They paddle down to the Oxbow, where Roosevelt shoots a wood duck, then walk about 15 miles, partly overland, to a crude farmhouse in the woods. Food is plain but there is good milk, and with a rabbit and a partridge taken on the way they supply their own meat.

events.detail: Paddles to the Oxbow and walks 15 miles to a backwoods house
Takes a wood duck, a rabbit and a ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: we have shot our own meat

headline: Twenty miles to a cranberry-bog pond
summary: Roosevelt walks over 20 miles round trip through the woods to a bog pond ringed with cranberries, shooting a duck there and picking up two grouse and a hawk along the way.

events.detail: Long walk to a bog pond; shoots a duck, two grouse and a hawk

tr_quotes.text: The walking was pretty good.

headline: Footsore return to Island Falls
summary: A 25-mile walk through the forest brings Roosevelt back to Island Falls, past waterfalls in deep ravines, with five grouse shot on the way. One moccasin is nearly worn through and his feet are sore.

events.detail: Walks about 25 miles back to Island Falls
Shoots five ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: Wore one of my moccasins almost out, which made me rather footsore.

headline: Admiring the Yankee backwoodsmen
summary: Roosevelt attends church, reads his Bible and spends the day shaving, bathing and readying for another expedition. He praises the backwoods meeting houses and the hunters, lumbermen and farmers of the region. To Bamie he writes that the Katahdin outing was luxury next to this second trip.

events.detail: Attends a backwoods church and reads his Bible
Prepares for a new expedition
Letter to Bamie about the hard Munsungan trip

letters.topic: Compares his rugged second trip with the Katahdin outing

tr_quotes.text: I don't know a better or more intelligent race of men than these shrewd, plucky, honest Yankees - all of them hunters, lumbermen or small farmers.
our trip to Katahdin was absolute luxury.

headline: Rained in
summary: Steady rain keeps Roosevelt from starting out.

events.detail: Delays departure because of rain

tr_quotes.text: Rained all day, so did not start.

headline: Rough road, rougher cabin
summary: Roosevelt and Bill Sewall set out by wagon behind an unruly horse over bad roads, stopping after about 30 miles at a very crude cabin.

events.detail: Thirty-mile wagon trip with Sewall to a backwoods cabin

tr_quotes.text: Started with Bill, in a rough wagon with a rougher horse; the roads were rougher still; and the cabin we are now staying in, after going about 30 miles, is roughest of all.

headline: A welcome at Littlefield's clearing
summary: Roosevelt walks about 25 miles through the woods to a backwoods homestead run by a settler named Littlefield, who looks after them well. He shoots spruce grouse in a spruce thicket and a tamarack swamp.

events.detail: Walks about 25 miles to Littlefield's clearing
Shoots two spruce grouse

tr_quotes.text: where we were very well treated.

headline: Tough as a pine knot
summary: Walking back to the horse, Roosevelt kills four grouse, then drives to Island Falls and shoots a pigeon from the wagon. Two weeks of foul weather have not dampened him; he feels superbly healthy.

events.detail: Walks back to the wagon and drives to Island Falls
Kills four grouse and a pigeon

tr_quotes.text: as tough as a pine knot.

headline: To the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: Roosevelt walks through the woods to the lower end of Mattawamkeag Lake, where he camps.

events.detail: Walks to the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake

tr_quotes.text: Walked down through the woods

headline: Seven grouse from one flock
summary: On a 20-mile walk Roosevelt takes two partridges on a hemlock ridge and then seven from a flock of eight in a river meadow. At rifle practice that afternoon he shoots well, though Dow and Sewall shoot better.

events.detail: Kills nine ruffed grouse on a 20-mile walk
Rifle practice with Dow and Sewall

tr_quotes.text: I shot very well, but not as well as Dow and Seawall.

headline: Luxury and hardship, both enjoyed
summary: Roosevelt paddles to Island Falls for the night and packs to leave. A porcupine that wanders into camp is chased off with a tin dipper. He marvels at the swings of his year between high living and hard toil, both of which he loves.

events.detail: Paddles to Island Falls and packs up
Drives a porcupine out of camp with a dipper

tr_quotes.text: What glorious fun I am having this year!
And my life has such absurd contrasts. At one time I live in the height of luxury; and then for a month will undergo really severe toil and hardship - and I enjoy both extremes almost equally.

headline: Down the Mattawamkeag by birchbark
summary: Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow start down the Mattawamkeag in a birch canoe, covering about ten miles below the lake. He and Dow circle through the woods to ambush a flock of mergansers, and he misses some long rifle shots at loons and cranes. He will hate to end the trip but is eager to get back to Harvard.

events.detail: Canoes down the Mattawamkeag River
Ambushes mergansers with Dow; misses long shots at loons and cranes

tr_quotes.text: I shall be very sorry to end this trip; and yet how I shall enjoy getting back to Harvard.

headline: Camp below Wytopitlock
summary: The canoe party paddles past Wytopitlock and camps. Dow shoots well at ducks and pigeons while Roosevelt misses most, but he redeems himself with rifle shots at hawks and owls. Muskrat and merganser both prove good eating.

events.detail: Paddles down past Wytopitlock and camps
Shoots poorly at birds but well at hawks and owls with the rifle

tr_quotes.text: both it + the fish ducks were very good eating!

uncertain: Source spells it 'Wytipitlock'.

events.detail: Testifies before the Judiciary Committee for dissolving the Manhattan Elevated Railway

tr_quotes.text: There is a strong and growing feeling of indignation among the people at the actions of these great corporations . . . it is incumbent upon us to see that this feeling takes a lawful shade.
If it becomes evident that these great public robbers cannot be reached by law, then among the people at large the temptation to take action that is outside the law becomes very strong.

For the sake of protecting honest capital, we ought to punish, if we legally can, the deeds of the dishonest wealthy for fear that someday an uprising might come that will overwhelm innocent and guilty alike.
